svg.title: Airport lighting at night
svg.desc: Four rotating beacon color combinations for civilian land airports, water airports, heliports and military airports, notes on when the beacon operates, a plan view of a runway with white, amber and red edge lights, REIL flashing lights and a taxiway with blue edge and green centerline lights, and who controls airport lighting at towered and non-towered airports.
svg.text: Airport lighting is standardized, so every airport uses the same light colors for runways and
taxiways. The type of lighting depends on how busy and complex the airport is.
Rotating beacon: the colors tell you the type of airport
Beacons help a pilot identify an airport at night and are normally operated from dusk until dawn.
Sometimes they are on when the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet and/or ground visibility is less than 3
statute miles, but there is no requirement, so the pilot must decide whether the weather meets VFR minimums.
The beam is most effective from 1 to 10 degrees above the horizon, though it can be seen well above or below.
Runway edge lights outline the runway at night or in low visibility: HIRL (high), MIRL (medium) and LIRL (low
intensity). HIRL and MIRL have variable intensity settings.
They are white, except on instrument runways, where amber lights mark the last 2,000 feet or half the runway,
whichever is less. The lights marking the end of the runway are red.
REIL: a pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the runway threshold, for rapid and positive
Taxiway edge lights are blue and outline the taxiway. Some airports also have green taxiway centerline
lights. Edge lights may have variable intensity, adjusted by ATC when needed or on request.
Airport lighting is controlled by ATC.
A pilot may ask ATC or FSS to turn light systems on
or off and to set a specified intensity, if
The lights may be on a timer, or FSS staff may
control them where an FSS is on the airport.
